flawed_step: The only natural route is to turn the closed Euler trail, which uses every edge, into a cycle through every vertex. That step can't be justified. An Euler trail may pass through a vertex more than once, and neither even degrees nor 2-connectivity stops a graph from being "unbalanced." For example, a bipartite graph with parts of different sizes has no Hamiltonian cycle.
counterexample: G = K_{2,4}. Vertices a, b on one side and x1, x2, x3, x4 on the other; the edges are a–xi and b–xi for i = 1..4 (8 edges, simple graph). Degrees: deg(a) = deg(b) = 4 and deg(xi) = 2, all even. G is connected, so it is Eulerian. One Euler circuit: a x1 b x2 a x3 b x4 a. 2-connected: G has 6 ≥ 3 vertices. Deleting a leaves b joined to every xi, so the graph stays connected; deleting b is the same by symmetry. Deleting some xj leaves a and b joined through any other xi, and every remaining xi touches both, so the graph stays connected. Not Hamiltonian: G is bipartite, so any cycle alternates between the two sides and uses equally many vertices from each. A cycle through all 6 vertices would need 3 from each side, but one side has only 2 vertices. So there is no Hamiltonian cycle.
assessment_summary: The statement is false. K_{2,4} is a simple graph that is 2-connected with all degrees even (4 and 2), so it is Eulerian. It is bipartite with parts of sizes 2 and 4, so it has no Hamiltonian cycle. The attempted proof fails at the step that would turn an Euler circuit into a Hamiltonian cycle.
